title: NVIDIA pushes the physical-AI stack at GTC Berlin: Isaac OS, Isaac Lab 3.0, and a reference humanoid
subtitle: Jensen Huang's October 21 keynote at the Tempodrom paired an open-source robotics runtime with Agile Robots' Agile ONE SN and European partners from ABB to KUKA.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: At the Tempodrom in Berlin on October 21, NVIDIA used the GTC keynote to broaden its physical-AI stack. Isaac OS, an open-source runtime built on NVIDIA Holoscan, is now generally available, as is Isaac Lab 3.0, the training-and-refinement framework that runs on everything from a laptop GPU to a data-center cluster and supports multi-GPU workflows with the Newton and NVIDIA PhysX physics engines. Alongside the software, Agile Robots announced the Agile ONE SN, a 1.40-meter, 40-kilogram reference humanoid built on NVIDIA Isaac GR00T and Jetson Thor, with 31 degrees of freedom and a 3-kilogram per-arm payload, scheduled for early 2027. NVIDIA also released the SimReady Central Library of more than 2,000 simulation assets and the Human 1M Dataset.

The point of the stack is to collapse the gap between simulation and the factory floor. Isaac Lab 3.0 is where the policy is trained, Isaac OS is what runs it on the robot, and the simulation libraries supply the pre-labeled scenes and human-motion data needed to pre-train policies before any hardware is touched. Making all three open source and tying them to Jetson Thor silicon is NVIDIA's play for the general-purpose humanoid wave the way CUDA was its play for the deep-learning wave — own the toolchain early, let partners build the hardware, keep the compute standard.

The partner list is a tell on strategy. European industrial automation names — ABB Robotics, KUKA, NEURA Robotics, Sereact — are building on the platform, which is why the launch is in Berlin and not San Jose. The physical-AI frontier is shifting from research labs to the companies that already supply arms, control cabinets, and factory lines; NVIDIA wants to be the Linux of that stack rather than the Boston Dynamics. Agile Robots' Agile ONE SN is explicitly a reference design, not a product line — the aim is to give the industry something to copy from, not to sell robots.

A takeaway for learners: a stack is a strategy. When a vendor releases a runtime, a training framework, and a reference hardware spec in the same keynote, read it as the attempt to standardize a layer that nobody has standardized yet. If you are evaluating a career move into robotics, pay attention to which pieces of the stack are open source (Isaac Lab, Isaac OS) and which are not (Jetson Thor, GR00T weights). The open parts become shared vocabulary; the closed parts become the vendor's moat. Both tell you where the industry is headed.
